reviews.text: For a fast review, only read the 'short review' part. This game is not for normal 'building games - gamers'. It is a roge-like game. It is something quite unique, so I would suggest that you read some reviews before buying it. Chapter 2+ are some edited parts of my old review. The short review is updated on 24_7_21. 1.) Short review 2.) Mistakes (player made) 3.) Spiral of death 4.) Fight - nothing good here 5.) Fly away. Sounds good, doesn't work. 6.) Last words [hr][/hr] 1.) Short review +) It is a [u][b]roge-like city builder[/b][/u]. That is something we haven't seen a lot and is something quite unique. +) The grafics are good (if you like the style like me) +) The [u][b]wave difficulty is pretty good balanced.[/b][/u] +-) Researching everything and beating the game takes about [u][b]15h-20h playtime.[/b][/u] +-) The [u][b]UI is not good not bad.[/b][/u] You have to switch between different layers/modes a bit more then necessary. 'Add-on' overview is missing. -+) [u][b]A lot of stress/pressure.[/b][/u] This is a roge-like city builder, where the enemies get stronger and stronger over time. Since you start with a very low difficulty, you don't realise it right from the start, but it will bite your butt later. If you are to slow in the first 5h, you will die after 10h. Every second matters. This is normal for roge-like games and some people like this, but most 'building games - gamers' doesn't. Expect to loose your city. -) [u][b]The building is very clunky.[/b][/u] They don't tell you in the tutorial, that you can copy buildings with 'v'. The buildings in the building menu look very similar. You have space problems and no time to do space-management. ([i]last patch they increased it a little bit[/i]) -) [u][b]Fighting. Nothing good here.[/b][/u] Very few weapons, items. No movement abilities. Brainless enemies. No tactics. This is especially bad, since you will fight for around 50% of the time. -) [u][b]You rebuild 50%-80% of your buildings.[/b][/u] This means you need 50% of your time fighting and getting new ressource nodes. 30% of the time to rebuild lost buildings and activate/deactive buildings. Only 20% of your time having fun with new resources/buldings. Combined with the stress this is why I wrote in my first rewiev: [u][b]It is even worse then work.[/b][/u] -) [u][b]The defense is brainless too.[/b][/u] upgrading towers is way to expensive and also not expensive enough to take them with you. When a raid attacks you, you just build 5-20 towers with walls infront and they kill the wave with you. thats it. no tactics. no way to make it better. no skill involved. -) [u][b]You are always one mistake away from loosing everything.[/b][/u] When they break through, you lose. There is nothing you can do. There are many small reasons how this can happen. To few flux for building towers. Enemies taking another path then anticipated. Forgot to activate the towers. (you deactive them between waves to save flux/power) You were outside and didn't make it home in time. -+) The 'Add-on' design is a bit strange. I am happy, that they removed it from starwood etc. , but they still have it everywhere else. When you install an add-on, the basic recipe costs way more upkeep/workers (like 200% to 400% more) for the same output. This is confusing at first. [hr][/hr] 2.) Mistakes (player made) Mistakes are unforgiving. That is a problem, but combined with the bad design, it becomes a big problem. There are many ways and also hidden ways (like installing 'add-ons') to make mistakes. Every mistake can be fatal, because every second counts, which makes it very frustrating. You have to start over a lot, or try to push further only to lose your base later to the ever increasing difficulty. [i]edit: You start with a very easy difficulty on default. I am bit concerned about mid/late-game. Every mistake sums up... [/i] 3.) Spiral of death [strike]Currently, this game is not balanced.[/strike] Even if it would be balanced, the game has a 'Spiral of death' in its design. What do I mean with that? The difficulty of the next wave can't be predicted. [strike]There are huge jumps in HP/difficulty.[/strike] When you lose even a part of your town, it is game over. [u][b]These 3 things combined are a nightmare [/b][/u] When you lose even a part of your town, you can only flee. Rebuilding defense/economy is not only impossible, it also makes no sense economically. This means you flee to the next sector, where the enemies are stronger and your town is weaker ..... [i]edit: After 5h playtime, you can't lose a part of your city. You defend or you loose everything[/i] It is better to just start over (again), then to fall into the spiral of death, where the enemies get stronger and you stay the same or even get weaker and weaker. 4.) Fight - nothing good here Making fighting fun is very hard. Even games like factorio failed here. But in this game it looks like the dev's didn't even try. No special move abilities. Very few weapons. Simple and boring enemies. And more .... I dont see any positive thing here. I dont expect it to be as good as in 'The Riftbreaker', but this .... 5.) Fly away. Sounds good, doesn't work. A flying city sounds good at first, but has many problems. The biggest one I had with it is that you build the same thing over and over again. There is not a lot of new things you can do. To throw some random numbers in: more then 80% of the stuff you build are buildings you lost while fleeing. If you played factorio just imagine rebuild green science every 30min without blueprints. Or even better blue science (inclusive oil produciton). These 80% have to go down! Or other things have to happen to make it less of a burden. [i]edit: Later, it is 'only' 50% ....[/i] In 'mindustry' for example it is similar, but it feels much better. You nearly have every map a new resource and new enemies / units. Even new gamemodes are hidden in it. (base vs base instead of wave-defense) You can even use old bases for research or later also send resources to the frontline. It is also a bit stressful to start a new sector, but you never lose everything. You also have a lot of new things/resources to play with with every new sector. The only downsides are the graphics and the difficult late-game. 6.) Last words Overall it is balanced and not slim (20h+) , but since you do roughly 80% of the time something boring ..... it is by far not 30 bucks worth. When they optimize building and make fighting at least a bit challanging/fun, it will maybe the 30 bucks worth.

游戏的理念很有趣，保留核心建筑转移位置。目前我在新手图撑了到等级15，刚转移新图。游玩过程中我发现了几个问题： 1.木墙跟纸糊的一样，可以考虑增加木墙的防御力 2.可以提示目前资源，我研究出新资源后，找了好几圈才猜测应该是新手图没有这资源，而不是出现了BUG 3.存在非建造区，建议将边界的植物改为玩家可以自由修改，这样我可以手动设计怪物的前进路线，同一张图可以撑的更久，也会更有趣 目前大问题就是这些，不过引导可能有些缺失，如果不是拥有丰富的同类游戏经验，我可能最开始也有点搞不清楚大部分工厂的功能，包括模块的增加，生产物品的改变，可以增加引导来展示这些变化

If you're thinking about purchasing hold off for now but keep your eye on it. While there are some good things about Dream Engines: Nomad Cities, the core mechanics need major polishing and refinement. My criticisms: -Core loop doesn't do anything to stand out from other titles in the same genre/type and lacks depth. -Combat and exploration mechanics are lackluster, bare bones, and frustrating. -The timer... I felt like I was "on the clock" at a job and it made me anxious. -No floating cities actually... you teleport from zone to zone but never get to experience a flying citadel of your creation. -Animations for combat need a lot of work. -So many menus... and once the raid starts you better hope you have everything where you need it because you won't be able to do a thing (why can't workers repair things?). -With such a beautiful art style, it's a shame that exploring is boring and drab. I like the concept but I think the devs need to consider ways to implement mechanics that will separate them from every other Factorio-like resource builder.

[u][b]Introduction[/b][/u] One of my biggest mispurchases during the last year when it became available. The major problem i have with it, its insanely boring to play. It features super generic enemies, environments and gameplay systems. Its worst flaw however is to take too strong inspiration on the bad parts of other games, to then constantly deny its a trainwreck because of it. So lets dig down the rabbit hole...or whatever...to find out why it ended up like that. I know its a lot of text, but bare with me, i go through several connected points explaining why its design is illogical as soon as you take it apart. And by doing so, i will try to explain you in detail how it appears to me when playing, besides just being insanely boring. [b]For a TLDR focus on the highlighted points in the text.[/b] [u][b]The Games Problematic Design[/b][/u] See, the general premise of building a city to a randomly created location, sending out units to harvest its resources, while preparing to defend and process those resources to expand the city, is a really great one. It promises risk-reward decisions, it promises strategic gameplay, it promises endless content and challenge. The reality is though, that [b]most of the time is spent by walking around with an uninspired Robot Avatar.[/b] You are [b]NOT[/b] sending out units to harvest resources from mines or chopping wood or do whatever, in fact, there are no units to use for that. You are [b]NOT[/b] sending out anything to fight the enemies and holding them back. You have to manually shoot them with your robot, with the most boring and sluggish combat experience to be ever created for videogames. You will [b]NOT[/b] spend a lot of time managing your city and building on it to expand. You will be busy manually exploring an empty map with generic environments, shooting generic enemies with unsatisfying weaponry, as a stupid robot. See, there are games out there doing basically the same, Factorio or Dyson Sphere Program to name just two. But both of these games do a much better job of finding a balance between doing something manually, and actually automating so you dont have to. The other major problem of taking inspiration from those games by [u]forcing an Avatar System into the game is ignoring that those games have factual problems utilizing it properly[/u]. The combat in Factorio is easily the worst part about the entire game. Theres tons of things you could take inspiration of from Factorio or Dyson Sphere Program. [u]The Avatar Mechanic however, is exactly not that part you should be inspired by.[/u] [u][b]In Comparison[/b][/u] Now to the next point, there already exists such a game with Airborne Kingdom. You would correctly state that both games are different besides a flying city and moving across a map to exploit the regions. Yes and No. Yes, because there are things done differently and honestly, thats in favor of Airborne Kingdom and opposed to Dream Engines. Airborne Kingdom didnt receive gameplay mechanics that just make the gameplay sluggish, boring and unenjoyable by simply focussing on whats interesting and fun, but scrapping what is just a burden of loaded garbage piled on top. And No, because both share enough similarities so you could easily forget about Dream Engines and play any of the superior alternatives out there, without missing anything. Dream Engines doesnt offer anything unique to justify its current existence. [b]As long as they try to embrace a feature that keeps the gameplay to shift focus from the fun parts to the tedious and annoying parts, it wont become any good enough to be worth your money, or more important, your time.[/b] Currently playing DreamEngines is an experience of using a double edged sword cutting you no matter how you hold it. [b][u]The fun part is building the city[/u][/b], processing materials, finding a balance between what to take with you and what to leave behind. [b][u]The bad part is the entire rest of the game[/u][/b], the exploration, the Robot controlling, the combat, the defending, the boring environments, the pointless weapons to research for an Avatar you dont want to play anyway. Sadly the latter, meaning the bad part, is the majority of the game and its entire focus. I could forgive if those parts were short and only occasional annoyances dragging me away from the good parts of the gameplay, but they arent. They are what you do the most. If they scrapped it, the game would lose quite a bit of content. But thats what you get when you invest too much time into the obviously worst part of your game, while ignoring the good parts of it. And this core problem leads me to the next point. [u][b]Final Thoughts, Recommendations and Expectations[/b][/u] The result is, that even the good parts of the game feel underdeveloped, undercomplex and rather boring. This game thus ended up in a hate relationship with two gameplay systems. On one hand you have the city management on the other you have an RPG. Both hate each other, but if you delete one of them you only end up having a pile of unrefined garbage, too boring to be called a game. And so the Avatar Gameplay is necessary. Its necessary to cover the fact that the entire rest of the game, the city management, isnt capable of keeping the game flying for too long. You need the ugly robot and the ugly combat, the boring as hell exploration and grindy feeling of exploiting or fighting, so that it can cover up the fact that the city management is as shallow. You need the ugly robot to let the city management appear great in contrast although it isnt if you would look at it as an isolated system. To me, speaking as someone spending an excessive amount playing strategy games and designing gameplay systems myself, this game feels like someone should have decided to scrap a few things early on in the concept phase. Some person standing at the drawing board looking at the post-its splattered around should have had the gutts to say: [b]"Guys, screw that part entirely and focus on this part of the game to make it much better. This Avatar is just distracting from the core experience and ends up being a misplaced load dragging the rest of the game down."[/b] [u]But no one had the gutts to say that.[/u] And so Dream Engines sounds astonishingly great on paper but fails horribly as a game. Here its clear that there has been an oversight in the concept stage. And it appeared far too often to myself in tunnel vision when having spent a lot of time designing a unique gameplay mechanic or entire game and then having to accept at a late stage, - that it just doesnt work out, - that its not fun, - that its too oppulent to be feasable, - that one mechanic might sound cool and fun but just obstructs the entire rest of the game. [b]And at these moments, i do the one thing that needs to be done, i take that gameplay mechanic, drag it down into the cellar, and kill it. At first it hurts to have wasted time to make it fit, to make it barely work, but to save the rest of the game it needs to die for good.[/b] Its dead weight, so get rid of it. [u][b]Conclusion[/b][/u] In my eyes, Dream Engines will very unlikely lift up to become a great game. It might become an OK game after tons of work has been done. It might become acceptable and in fact, maybe they even manage to refine the game so much that the bad parts of it wont weight too much anymore. Possibly shifting the balance from mostly bad to mostly good. >Yet i am sceptical and recommend you to wait it out.< As its high priced and even at half its price isnt worth it. If you love games like Factorio or Dyson Sphere, or They are Billions, or whatever, dont. It cant compete against any of those, not even when they were in Alpha Stage and believe me, i have played the ugly version of Factorio you can see on Indiegogo. Dream Engines is far away to even meet that level of fun.

For those who might wonder how the game play is, I'll give you a short explanation based on my experience. To simply say, it's a base-building, survival game which seems influenced by Tim Burton movies. As a robot leader managing a nomad city, your main goal is to survive, feed your people and upgrade the city by producing and utilizing tons of dreamy resources like ink-flavoured potatoes, bloodwood logs, nightmare juice, etc. You also need to build your own defense system because the outside of the city is full of nightmare creatures which constantly try to invade your city. After you reach a certain point, however, the number of these creatures increases exponentially and you won't be able to hold them any longer. In the end, this gives you no choice but to make the city float in the air, which means it's time to leave and move the whole city to somewhere! Then you choose which biome your city starts with and what kind of risks to take since every biome has different types of resources but monsters living in there will not exactly be the same as the previous ones. Once the city successfully lands on the new biome, you repeat all the process above hoping your city survives longer and works more efficiently than before. That's it! Now here's what I'm gonna say. To be honest, I cannot recommend this for someone looking for well polished city builder games because it's true that lots of things listed on the roadmap are missing and it seems the game still has a long way to go. However, considering it takes one to two years until full release and even a couple of hours of the game play offered me joyful experience, I'm quite satisfied at this state and I think it's ok to give it thumbs up! If you are a huge fan of Tim Burton or just tempted with the whimsical atmosphere of the game, this one might be just for you :D 관심을 가지고 있을법한 유저들을 위해서 직접 플레이한 경험을 바탕으로 짧게나마 설명을 해보자면, 이 게임은 서바이벌 도시 건설 장르를 채용한 작품으로, 팀 버튼 감독의 영화로부터 많은 영향을 받은 작품이라 할 수 있다. 게임의 주 목표는 바로 꿈 속 유랑 도시를 운영하는 것. 플레이어는 이 도시의 관리자로서 시민들을 먹이고 생존을 도모함과 동시에 도시를 성장시키는 역할을 수행하게 되는데, 이를 위해서는 잉크맛 감자, 혈나무, 악몽 주스와 같은 다양한 꿈속 자원을 채취하고 이를 최대한 효율적으로 활용해야만 한다. 게다가 운영적 측면 외에 방어 체계를 구축하여 도시를 보호하는 일도 수행해야 하는데, 도시 바깥 지역은 악몽 괴물로 가득한데다가 이들은 끊임없이 도시를 침공하려들기 때문. 시간이 어느정도 경과하면 도시를 침공하는 괴물들의 개체수가 기하급수적으로 늘어나기 시작하며, 플레이어의 힘만으로는 도저히 감당할 수 없는 상황에 이르게 된다. 마지막에 할 수 있는 일이라고는 재빨리 도시를 하늘로 띄워버리는 것 뿐인데, 바로 이 시점에 플레이어는 도시를 통째로 이전함으로써 다음 지역으로 넘어갈 수 있게 된다. 어떤 지형에 정착할지에 대한 선택권은 별도로 주어지지만, 지형 별 채집 가능한 자원이나 출몰하는 악몽 괴물이 모두 다르기 때문에 선택에 따라서 안고 가야할 리스크 역시 달라지는 편. 도시가 성공적으로 새로운 장소에 착륙했다면, 이후에는 더 효율적이면서도 긴 시간 동안 생존이 가능하도록 신경써가면서 다시 한번 위에서 언급한 과정을 반복하기만 하면 된다. 소개는 이쯤에서 마무리하고, 이제 솔직하게 평을 내려보자면 잘 만든 시티 빌더 게임을 원하는 사람들에게 추천하기에는 시기상조인 감이 있다. 개발자가 공개한 로드맵에서 아직 구현되지 않은 것이 많은데다가 게임 자체는 갈 길이 멀어 보이기 때문이다. 그러나 해당 게임이 얼리엑세스 기간을 1~2년으로 길게 잡고 있다는 점, 미완성 게임임에도 불구하고 그 몇시간 조차 즐거운 경험이었다는 점을 고려하면, 현 상태 만으로도 상당히 만족스러운 수준이기에 당장은 긍정적으로 평가를 내리려 한다. 팀 버튼 감독의 팬이거나 게임 특유의 기괴한 분위기가 매력적으로 느껴진다면 재밌게 즐길 수 있는 게임이니 참고하시길.

[code] “我与许多人一样，对‘游牧民族’最初的兴趣来自于一些浪漫想象。游牧人群逐水草而居，过着自由不羁的生活———风吹草低见牛羊，是中国文人对这种无拘无束生活的浪漫写照。然而，人类学所见的游牧社会首先便让我们摆脱这些浪漫想象，强调这是人们利用边缘、不稳定自然资源的一种经济、社会生态体系——生活中处处充满危机与不确定，毫无浪漫可言。” ——摘自《游牧者的抉择》 [quote]关注[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/36224058/]老实人鉴赏家 [/url] 老实人评测，不错过游戏的闪光点，不放过游戏的吐槽点，带给玩家最直观的测评感受。[/quote] 初次接触这个游戏的我就被游戏名以及介绍深深吸引——《梦幻引擎：游牧城市》，具有飞行能力的游牧城市，这可比哈尔的移动城堡听起来酷多了（不提传送魔法的话），我未来打造可是移动的空中花园。而事实上，却如我引用的那段话，浪漫的终究是想法，现实却不尽人意。如果硬要找点趣味，自动化是科技的浪漫，怪物是末世的梦幻，也说得过去。 [h1] 地块选择，说则飞行，实则定点迁徙[/h1] 不同于常规的城市建造经营游戏，一上来就大地图，各种格式的资源等着采集研究。本作中将没有常规的大地图，而是由各个小型地块组成，这些地块资源种类、数量、怪物等级、附加值全都不同。每个地块资源种类虽然不多，胜在数量上不缺，需要自行探索地图找到资源点，并建立采集点传送回来加工。没有地块将会是你的绿洲，它们没有齐全且无限的资源，并且随着回合的流逝，怪物袭击的等级也将逐渐加强，它们只能是你的中转站，而核心就是属于你的“飞行城市”。 游戏分为两种建造区域，一种是城市内区域，二是城市外地块。顾名思义，飞行城市内地块的建筑是可以带走的，而城市外的建筑则在移动时舍弃。游戏开始的城市区域并不大，但也能够建造齐全维持城市运转的各种建筑。虽然资源没有太缺，但不想反复调整布局，大致的区域布置还得规划，同时也得考虑飞行后城市内建筑是否能维持资源正常运转。 地图散落着许多怪物，可以操纵机器人进行远程&近战攻击。每隔一段时间会有怪物强袭，强袭的等级会随着时间的增长而增加。初始几次强袭等级都很低，资源足够后也可以建造升级炮台保护基地，后期强袭的怪物数量多、还有攻高血厚的怪物夹杂在其中，在一个地块停留过久不是一个好的选择。 科技树解锁之后，机器人上的远程、近战、护甲都可以升级，科技树也是围绕着几种主要建筑运用新的材料升级强化。游戏初期经常会遇到无法建造或无法升级的建筑，只能将该地块资源收集完成后换地块找新资源，所以只想安静专心的发展是不可能的。不过游戏可以选择取消强袭，就看玩家自己选择了，但毕竟是不同于其他游戏的设计内容，个人还是建议体验。 [h1]游戏玩法尚可，细节与平衡还得琢磨[/h1] 这种带点怪物袭击的玩法，生存感和紧迫感倒是都带动出来了，建筑经营的点也算到位，但没有一项是能够让玩家深入研究的。房屋人口和各建筑的关系，看起来就像是每个游戏玩法都是这样的，所以我也得有。但实际效果就是，工人效果没体现出来，反正就是缺人，有点流于表面。建造建筑时不能暂停，有时候想研究下布局，还得先应付怪物的攻击，虽然建筑都可以移动，但是我要暂停！暂停！暂停功能啊！！ 游戏目前的内容比较全面，制作组也在根据玩家反馈不断的优化细节，更新线路图也规划了许多新的内容，就游戏体验而言，还是值得一玩的。当然，我想要的的空中花园是建不出来了，好歹弄个移动堡垒，再不济整个自动化生产工厂也行吧。 [/code]

[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/38287879]网易UU鉴赏家培养计划[/url][/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] 来这里找优质游戏、开黑日友、白嫖UU时长卡 [/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] 加速Steam社区、游戏记得用UU哦_(:з」∠)_ [/th] [/tr] [/table] [/quote][/h1] 它的游戏风格不太好描述，工业革命带来了大型自动化生产线，但建筑大多数还是使用木板搭建而成，它处于中世纪木制建筑和蒸汽朋克科技与魔幻之间，有种无主之地一样的无厘头。 而我们要控制的机器人小迪，就是个木头疙瘩制成的全能型机器人，既要维持城市运营，又要和场景中的怪物进行战斗以扩张，像极了我们墨家的机关之术。 [h1]会飞的工业城镇与流水线[/h1] 刚刚进入游戏，这熟悉的UI界面让我有一种穿越到了Klei的游戏里，熟悉的字体和菜单风格。 正如上面所说，这个游戏拥有着大型自动化的工厂生产线，而所有资源的去向与支出都指向了一个地方，就是城镇的中心。 城镇的中心占格4✖4，也就是只有16条轨道能够连接到中心，不过所幸，如今游戏内容不算多，木材石材和食物等等原材料经过加工后产品种类也不多，能够绰绰有余的进行分流和产线扩张。 游戏可建筑地形分为三类，一类是城镇内部，也就是黑色区域均为城镇的地板，起飞时这上面的建筑会跟着一起走。所以这里的建筑大多数都是比较重要且核心的建筑，比如城市的中心、民居和科研建筑。 然后是黑色区域以外的土地，这里需要使用电塔供电后才能使用，就像星际争霸中神族的水晶塔，它会提供一定范围的建筑区域。大多数工业建筑和加工厂都在这些地方完成，并通过轨道运回中心。 接着就是城市游牧的目的了，资源方面的建筑，这些地方可能会远离城市，在没有电力的黑暗区域了，这里就需要玩家使用小迪去探索，并清空区域后才能在资源上方建筑，并通过轨道运到加工厂加工成产品。 在这款游戏里，民居需要消耗食品，但消耗量比输送量小很多，所以这条轨道经常是拥堵着的。而农场的生产也比加工的速度慢，所以三个农场都可能会喂不饱一个加工厂。木材与石材的采集却非常快，快到经常把产线堵着。 所以这就需要根据产速和产量来适当扩张产线和收缩产线，合理利用中心的16条轨道出入口。 这让我想起一款类似设定的轻游戏——异形工厂（Shapez.io），同样也是只有一个中心，却要提供出千奇百怪的加工重组后的形状，在这里产线分布问题就是比较考验玩家了。 除了最基本的建材——食物、木材、石材以外，游戏中还有不少比较新奇的资源。 游戏的主要消耗是幻能，这个是最基础的物资，所有最基本的建筑比如轨道都是需要幻能的，而解决这个资源问题只需要造一些幻能瓮就可以自产了，无需消耗其他资源，也无需连接轨道。 接着就是电能，这个是最搞玩家心态的物资了。由于工业设施消耗量巨大，玩家需要不断的造发电厂，造发电厂，造发电厂......可是发电厂占地很大且彼此之间不能相隔太近，每一次的扩充电能都需要开辟一处新的区域；建造费用很贵，需要大量的幻能和矿材。这要是和红警一样，苏联有个核能发电站就好了！（升级和科研可以提升发电效率） 接着就是焦油了，焦油是科研的基础，焦油和幻能可以转变成科技点，所以又需要再开辟一处焦油提炼及运输，综合起来科研正是耗电量的大魔王，却又不得不养着，因为只有科研才能提升发电的效率！ 同时，它还具备了塔防与策略的玩法。 游牧和殖民有些不同，又有些相似。他们都是在移动过程中进行烧杀抢掠，不过游牧仅仅只是抢走了资源，抢完后带上全部家当就跑。 于是，当玩家在一个地方猥琐发育了一定时间，当地的怪物会采取主动攻击，而这时玩家不仅要大力生产，还要想办法进行防御，围墙、箭塔等等，就像是在玩帝国时代黑森林地图。 而小迪除了建设和探索以外的另一个使命，就是主动迎战来袭的敌人，他们按波次和固定方向进攻，每一次刷新都会有所增强，所以单单靠小迪一个机器人是不行的，城市的城防建设要紧跟着生产线一起发展起来。 而当城市的城防建设实在扛不住的时候，就可以回到开头所说的，哈哈哈爷飞走啦！ [h1]总结[/h1] 说它是缝合怪吧，它都有一点点，游戏设计的还算是挺新奇，城市经营、塔防策略和工厂生产它都有。 唯一不足的点是内容比较少，建筑就那么几种，资源也就这么几种。前期是很不错的城市经营和工厂自动化产线设计，但剩下的就等资源收集好升级和升科技了。然后就完全变成一款塔防游戏和策略游戏，新鲜感一下子就过去了。 EA阶段发行至今已经半年却没有多大的变化，看着更新计划，只厂商希望可以持续制作下去，别爷飞走了！

[h1]带着自己的城市四处游牧飘荡[/h1] [h1]游戏初体验：在原有的玩法上略有创新[/h1] 游戏的整体玩法与《异星工厂》、《戴森球计划》等类似，整体的大框架还是工厂流水线模拟器，对于产能的配比是游戏的重中之重。但是如果只是依葫芦画瓢，那显然并不能算一个合格的游戏，本作的创新点从游戏名字上就已经可见一斑，‘游牧’城市，带着自己城市在不同的地图游牧获取资源就是在传统玩法上创新的点。 [h1][quote=] [table] [tr] [th] 欢迎关注 [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/38287879]网易UU鉴赏家培养计划[/url][/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] 来这里找优质游戏、开黑日友、白嫖UU时长卡 [/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] 加速Steam社区、游戏记得用UU哦_(:з」∠)_ [/th] [/tr] [/table] [/quote][/h1] [h1]实际游玩：易上手，但是有更多细节需要考虑[/h1] 本作是资源规划建设与战斗结合的游戏玩法，在大部分的情况下，玩家需要从地图上去寻找资源点采集运输到自己的城镇，以提供和支撑城镇的发展。同时在一定时间间隔之内，会有怪物进攻玩家的据点，这时候需要玩家进行战斗来保卫自己辛苦建立的城镇。 但是游戏新加的‘游牧’要素，让整个城镇建设过程分为了一段一段有始有终的任务。以寻找资源点降落为始，以起飞准备前往下一个资源点为终。在这一段一段的任务过程中，可以继承到上一次降落的东西只有在玩家城镇内的建筑以及一些加工过后的材料，而在城镇范围外的建筑物和采集到了原始资源则会随着城市的起飞而一同消失，在这个玩法的影响下，每次的起飞与降落就有了更加深入的考量，尽可能多的携带资源起飞当然是最好的，但是随着地图资源采集耗尽，产能下降，越多的资源代表着越长的时间，而越长的时间则代表着怪物进攻的强度会越来越高，如果超过了平衡点，可能会是游戏崩盘的开始。 抛开游戏自己的特色之外，再说一说这类游戏的共有的资源采集调配类玩法。游戏在这方面的玩法相较于同类游戏是略有弱化的，由于怪物进攻强度和资源采集产能干涸相对较快的关系，并没有很多的时间给玩家在一个地方铺设一套十分复杂的生产线，更多的是将地区附近的有限资源快速采集完毕之后，加工成可以携带的资源后进入下一个地图。游戏的生产建筑也相对来说比较少。虽然科技树做的很丰富，但是因为科技树是贯穿整个游戏的，所以科技树成为了选择降落地点的一个导向，而不是助力玩家建造更复杂的流水线的工具。 另外，值得一提的是由于玩家只能携带城市范围内的建筑起飞前往下一个资源点，而每个地图的资源点刷新位置都是不固定的，因此多了一个资源点和加工建筑之间路线不确定的变数。很大可能玩家每次降落会因为这个路线的关系而忙的焦头烂额，如果没有足够的预备资源快速建立传输带，那么游戏时间就会被大大的拉长，而拉长的代价就是怪物的进攻更加猛烈，这无疑是一个恶性循环的开始。 因此本作更加强调的是城市内的建筑布局，以及玩家对于下一个地图的提前资源规划和预估，在进入下一个地图的时候能够快速的重新建立起流水线采集资源，是能够顺畅体验游戏的关键点，也是本作属于游戏特色创新的地方。 [h1]游戏的不足：科技树较单一[/h1] 由于游戏玩法的限制，并不能像其他同类型游戏那样建立一个庞大的流水线网络，单人完成一个‘奇观’，加上城镇的地面有限，容纳建筑的数量被限制导致的结果就是无法建造很多的功能性建筑，因此科技树上大部分都是以强化玩家控制的建造者的战斗能力，和解锁更多的可采集资源的建筑为主，在强化流水线分拣、功能性建筑的深度上并不能做的很深，而科技树的单一也就导致了后续玩法注定不会有特别大的改变，游戏的体验也因为城镇的规模限制，并不能够得到较好的满足，每个地图之间除了资源和城镇建筑之外都比较孤立，在游戏体验上还有较大的提升空间。 [h1]总结：如果是相关游戏类型爱好者推荐入手[/h1] 如果对于同类的流水线资源规划类的游戏十分喜爱的玩家可以推荐入手，体验不一样的游戏玩法，和同类游戏的资源规划不同，本作更多的是要求玩家对于未来的资源有一定的规划，这样子的差异让游戏的新鲜感也有不一样的地方。 在有限的空间内进行规划建设，将游戏阶段目标以一个个地图明显分割开，都是本作的有改进的优点，但是因此导致了玩法较单一，新鲜感过去之后的游戏体验不像同类其他游戏那样好也是一个双刃剑的情况，这也是有待提高的地方。

Absolute gem, almost passed on it, but I'm so glad I didn't. Greatest twist on a factorio/city builder I've ever seen. It's so much fun! The negative reviews I'm seeing, particularly the top review, are either based on things before recent updates, or were players not knowing what they were doing. 1. You can pause the game. This gives you all the time you might want/need to fiddle with your base. 2. The game is one of the most forgiving city builders out there. Most of the basic structures, including "rails" (conveyor belts) cost nothing but "energy." You can move every single building (except walls and rails, and during attacks, towers). 3. The "stress" is what others might call excitement. As a new player, it might be "too stressful" without pause... but just pause the game if you want to read tooltips or micromanage/arrange your city. Press "F" for free camera and you can build anywhere on the map regardless of where Tiny is. 4. You can fit your most important buildings on the platform. Like, my setup, I mostly only rebuild farms and powerplants when I go to a new map. I haven't even had to build any balloons yet (an advanced building that lets your city carry more). There's also technologies you unlock that expand your platform. 5. There's a good variety of special moves and weapons to unlock in the tech tree and the advancement tree. I wouldn't want more, it would start getting to be too much of a juggling act... 6. The fighting is ARPG style (Diablo, Path of Exile, Midgard, DOTA/League, Warcraft 3, etc). If you hate that combat, you won't enjoy this combat.

Having played Dream Engines since it came into Early Access, some years ago, and again for several more hours following the "full release", I feel confident - and melancholy - in saying, it still does not spark joy. TL;DR - This game is not enjoyable. It has a very cool premise of great dream-powered cities soaring across a world haunted by strange nightmarish beings, which it completely fails to make an enjoyable game out of. Here are some of the things it still, after all those years of potential refinement, does so very wrong: [list][*]It gives you a slow, weak, boring robot who is barely animated, as your player character. Its walk cycle literally consists of South Park style wobbling. Weak, lazy, lame. [*]It forces you to engage in constant exploration and combat using said robot. This means walking until you encounter enemies, walking backward while shooting them with one of your lame crossbows, occasionally using melee attacks on a larger more heavily armored enemy. This gets old very quickly and is not particularly fun. [*]Enemies, like your robot, have little or no animation. There are flappy silhouettes that shoot and purple-spiked slugs that nibble. That's your lot for the first difficulty tier, which is hours and hours. [*]The building aspect of the game begins almost promisingly, but rapidly spirals into over-complexity and a stressful hell of trying to keep track of where to land so you can make the newest kind of wood, only to run out of the middle type of wood, only to land somewhere and find all the raw wood resource nodes are on the opposite side of the city from your wood processors. There's also stone, modifier resources like tar and acid, crystals that fit weirdly into various production processes. Way too many resources, and only a few of them on each map - so you constantly have to explore new areas, which -as previously mentioned- sucks. A lot. [*]A core gameplay rule of this game says "You can't store and transport raw, unprocessed resources." This, along with many similarly terrible design decisions, makes the game worse, more stressful, more anxiety-inducing and generally less playable. You can't just gather a bunch of acid from one place, combine it with wood in another area - you have to go to a place that has both of them, and combine them there before leaving with as much processed "acidwood" as you can produce. [*]The economy is psychotic. Almost every upgrade is either a sidegrade, featuring increased upkeep cost and other trade-offs so bad they feel like actual punishment in return for investing the upgrade materials, or a straight-up downgrade that makes the building worse on the whole. For instance, the rare upgrade module that makes processors "100% faster but consume 50% more materials". Translation: Pay three times as much input (150%x2) for twice as much output (100%x2). Why are you acting like this is a reward? Why did I pay rare scrap to craft this at a limited-use ruin? And this is not an exception, this is the norm. Every single upgrade or module is balanced to death so that the only real reason to upgrade anything is to achieve slightly better productivity without an increase in weight. You never have workers, food nor power to spare. To produce more of one, you need more of the others, and the production buildings are so inefficient they'll mostly just waste space for extremely minimal gains of excess power, workforce, etc. Utterly psychotic. [*]The upgrades that [i]are[/i] actual upgrades, cause buildings to consume additional resources. Early on, this is usually star tar, a weird substance pumped up from any region, though more efficiently in some and less in others. Thus, if you switch a power plant or two to star tar power, you make yourself reliant on landing in places that have enough of it - or on investing more city weight capacity (an extremely limited commodity), more workers and more power in building an extra tar well or two. Or upgrading them which also increases their need for said resources and manpower. So in addition to all the resources you need just to build and expand your city, you'll now be paying acidwood to do research at a tolerable rate in the mid-game, star tar for power, and so on and so forth. All with limited space and inefficient production mechanisms. You can get some passive bonuses over time to help, but they don't help enough. The economy is fundamentally broken. [*]Fuel for travelling between locations is limited. You have to explore ruined fuel depots and chemical plants to find more, at regular intervals, and if you ever DARE to add extra carry-weight capacity to your city with a single extra lifting balloon, you permanently increase the fuel cost of travel. Some locations don't have fuel at all. They could easily have just made it a fixed cooldown for city travel. Just one less insanely stressful thing to worry about all the time. But no. You have to scrounge fuel on top of everything, which yet again, means more terrible, boring, repetitive "combat" and "exploration" of the incredibly samey areas. There are more location types later on, sure. But will you bother playing long enough to even see them? Doubtful.[/list] I'm not sure what sort of person would enjoy this game. It's not nearly as good at being Factorio as, well, Factorio for starters. It's vastly worse as a base-building action exploration experience than The Riftbreaker, and looks infinitely worse despite a few weak attempts at visual appeal. It takes far too many bad ideas and runs deep into negative fun territory with them, where a competent designer would say "This doesn't work. The game is not fun. Let's rethink our mechanics." Deeply, and sadly, disrecommended.

[h1]怪物攻城？抱歉，我家会飞[/h1] 《梦幻引擎：游牧城市》是一款生存建造游戏。玩家将操控一个蒸汽机器人探索地图收集物资，建造一个又一个设施，增强自己的城市，从而抵抗幻魇的进攻。游戏中玩家要在一次性建筑和永久性建筑上进行取舍，当然要考虑自己的复工平台能不能容纳下那么多建筑。是保存资源，留到下一块领地再用？还是大肆挥霍与幻魇对抗到底？这一切都由你来选择。在正式版推出后也应广大玩家要求，推出了暂停的功能，甚至还添了个加速功能，还是很听劝的。 [h1]简单讲讲[/h1] 游戏初始一共有九个部落可以选择，每个部落都拥有自己的特性和debuff，不过除了最初的拾荒领主，其余八个都需要一些特殊条件才能解锁。游戏一共拥有八种难度可以选择，如果都不能满足你也可以选择自定义难度。进入游戏玩家将扮演一个蒸汽机器人，以俯视角来进行游戏，玩家可以在建造模式下自由的建造城市，离开城市去探索地图，寻找建造建筑所需要的资源。 [h1]战斗系统[/h1] 探索地图，寻找资源的途中自然少不了遇到敌人，而我们的敌人则是一只又一只长相怪异的幻魇，玩家可以通过左键近战攻击或者右键连弩攻击的方式应对。接着我们还可以解锁一些更高等级的装甲，或者解锁一些新的武器和副武器，也会解锁陷阱和更高级的防御塔。玩家如果在一个地图停滞太长时间，威胁等级就会提升，随之而来的就是更猛烈的幻魇突袭。所以游戏后期变成一个塔防游戏也不是不可能，好在只要起飞转换地图就会重置这个等级，所以还请大家自行考量在同一地图的停滞时间。 [h1]科研[/h1] 游戏在建造完科技实验室后投入对应物资就可以产出知识，依靠知识我们就可以在科技中进行升级。游戏前期的科技更注重于一些基础的物品和建筑图纸，而后期则是一些更高级的建筑图纸、更高效的生产机器、更高效的护甲与防御器械等等。我甚至还在科研比较后期的地方看见了增援部队的研究选项，不知道是否真的会造出一批机器人来帮忙对抗幻魇的袭击。 [h1]建造[/h1] 游戏主流玩法自然是城市建造，通过游戏的科研界面，我们就可以看见游戏丰富建筑图纸，除此之外，游戏在初期还会给予一部分图纸，而且在玩家的部落规模变大的同时，获得新的图纸、升级点以及扩张玩家的城市。而建造主要分为城市建造和一次性建造，城市建造就是指在万家的城市平台上可以带走的建筑物。而除此之外不能建造在玩家平台上的所有建筑物，都是一次性建筑物，大家要进行合理的取舍。而且游戏中物资的运输全部依靠传送带，所以自动化和城市美观也是大家需要考虑的事情。 [h1]最后来点碎碎念[/h1] 游戏的可玩性相当的高，无论是游戏丰富的建筑图纸，还是游戏丰富的玩法都能让一大部分人满意。而且游戏可移动城市，一次性建筑这些都算是比较创新的设定，个人感觉是很喜欢的。更何况这次正式版推出游戏不但更新了一部分内容，更是把玩家们都在期盼的暂停功能做了出来，还顺手做了个成就系统，态度也可谓是相当不错了。 [h1]总结[/h1] 总的来说，这是一款相当不错的生存建造游戏，游戏把沙盒生存、模拟经营、城市建造三种要素结合，还夹杂了一些塔防等元素，让这款游戏变得相当优秀，十分推荐大家购买尝试。 [quote]点击关注「 [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/41448772//]三言两语评测」→ [/url]简洁的语言，实用的内容 [/quote]

I tried, I really tried over the years with this game to the point I even started making an overhaul mod for it yesterday. But the issues with this game just run too deep. I bought this on day 1 of its early access, and the fundamental issues with this game have not been changed or fixed despite the feedback that has been left. It's not buggy at all, it's just bad. The premise of the game is wonderful, the execution is abysmal and it's down to the devs living in their own little bubble. Since this shares aspects with other games, i'll be comparing it to better explain my points. The only good thing that they've done is make the game easy to mod, but there are only like 10 mods for this game, and that's down to the fact that at its foundations, it is a badly designed game. Combat is boring and bad. Take The Riftbreaker(RB) as a prime example of combat done right. In Dream Engines (DE), your avatar is slow and weak. There is only ONE module slot for upgrades and other than the healing module, they're all useless. There is no experimentation to be had, or fun builds to make. The weapons are uninspired and they make combat incredibly slow. You are literally just pointing and holding down the mouse button to shoot at the enemies whilst backtracking so they don't destroy you when they get into melee range. Ironic considering there is a melee mod that also increases the damage you receive? Instant death if you use it. RB on the other hand has a fast paced engaging combat with a huge amount of experimentation to be had coupled with loads of fun weapons to try out. They even allow in the files to add more modules for the avatar... but this begs the question, why didn't the devs expand on the avatar and combat in the first place? Exploration is beyond tedious. With the maze like maps and time constraints along with the tedium of combat, it makes for an incredibly boring and dull experience. Every time you come across enemies which is every 10 seconds, you let out a sigh as you have to engage them in combat. This does not improve at all throughout the game because there are no upgrades that make it better. IF anything, it gets harder as enemies are swapped for more powerful ones. Compare that with RB where exploration was fun with the destructible environment compared with the fact that you often sought out enemies to slaughter because it was FUN. The city/factory building is convoluted with its numerous different resources, combined with the severe lack of space making it incredibly micro management intensive as you are constantly moving buildings, and swapping recipes. Harvesting and processing resources is slow and combine that with the fact that when you leave a map, raw resources get left behind. You won't find all the resources you need on 1 or even 2 maps, with maps missing resources you require. You essentially have to process as many resources as you can before you are overwhelmed by enemies and need to leave the map. This also makes the city building element incredibly slow. This would be fine since you are left with time to go and explore the maps...if it were not for the fact that as stated earlier, exploration and combat is BORING. A mix of factory/city building AND combat has been done twice before successfully at least from my own knowledge with Factory and The Riftbreaker which are both incredible games and fun in their own right. But it's like the devs from this game have never heard of either of those two games, let alone played them. The really sad thing is that the skeleton of a good game is there, but it would require a completely different approach from the developer and a significant overhaul to make the game good and fun because quite frankly, this game could be salvaged and be a success. - Reduce the micromanagement at the base - Remove the convoluted production chains - Make the Avatar fun to use in combat - Make exploration fun - Devs should actually go and play riftbreaker and factorio. Well, time to finally uninstall this game and remove it from my favourites as unless something changes significantly, I'll never ever be touching this again.

Ah man, it pains me to give a negative review... but this game has great ideas poorly executed. This is the loop: land on a map, secure the perimeter, secure the key production resource, explore (and clean) the map to access raw resource nodes, process raw resources, defend from raids until as long as you can, then take off and repeat. The concept is interesting, but the execution is not. There are three fundamental problems: 1. Exploring and cleaning the map is tedious. It's a chore since you just point at enemies and shoot, backtracking to avoid being overwhelmed in melee. The avatar is slow and has little customisation of weapons and plugins, so it's just not fun. 2. Micromanaging hell. Space in your city is limited, so you'll constantly move buildings and change recipes depending on the map you're in and the resources (not) available. Not all resources are available in each map, so you're constantly trying to balance workers availability, with flux availability, with power availability, with production volume... despite a huge variety of resources, it never felt I was making progress. Fix something and something else breaks. Production chains are varied and complex, but there's no real scalability of your base given the space and weight constrains and resources varying between maps. 3. Unbalanced roguelike mechanics. Which brings us to the third point. Once you land in a new map, you don't start from zero taking advantage of what's there (compare it with Against the Storm, for example), but you keep your consumption of flux, power, and food for workers. So every time I landed on a new map, it was a firefighting experience to stabilise those the production of those key resources, or everything else would break. Considering that there are plenty of modifiers to the production rates, and many vary depending on the map and the council head selected (valid for 50 cycles or so), and finding balanced production is impossible. Overall I researched on third of the (huge) tree and explored five maps, but eventually gave up due to the frustration given by stabilising the settlement when you land in any new map. As I said, the idea behind the game mechanics is good, but the realisation is not enough. Which is a shame. Get it with a discount (I got it with 50% off and don't regret the purchase) if you're curious to play it, or skip it altogether.

This game is almost something special, but fails to scale the difficulty properly. I disagree with most of the negative reviews, I think many of them are looking for a copy/paste of other games, while this game has a unique blend to makes it different from other games, which is why I enjoyed it for the first 20 hours. However, the real problem is that enemy strength scales faster than yoiur ability to defend your settlement does, meaning the longer you play, the harder it gets to defend yourself. At first, this feels like a nice challenge so you don't hit a point where you can rebuild the same basic defensive lines over and over and then breeze through the game, but eventually it gets to a point where it just feels frustrating because your defences are being destroyed faster than you can get the resources to rebuild them, on top of needing to build extra defences to prevent them being destroyed next time. The difficulty just scales at an unfair rate that feels frustrating rather than challenging. My personal experience was that despite being a very experienced gamer who doesn't typically have difficulty with games that people label as being difficult, I still frequently hit walls of feeling overwhelmed and shortly after finding a way to break through those walls, would soon hit another. I ended up just constantly trying to catch up, never able to advance. It's a real shame because I really enjoyed the game for a while.

I will recommend it because I had good enough time. But the game has some issues with dragging on near the end and a strange upgrade system. People who like to replay these types of games and challenge themselves maybe won't feel it as much. But for me I couldn't really finish the game because of these things. 1. The way building upgrades work, especially with power, flux and workers is... weird. It is almost always more efficient to just spam low lvl buildings instead of upgrading them. Sure, you can't take them with you but at the same time taking upgraded power buildings seems like a waste since they consume so much more power/resources and workers with the advanced recipes. And I mean it. Base power plant with the default recipe will require 3 workers to produce 10 power. While an upgraded building with an advanced recipe will require 24 workers and produce 60 power - you see where the problem is? I found it very counterintuitive. I want to make my city better but at the same time I felt like the game was penalizing me for it. Very weird system. 2. Enemies, waves, defending. It worked great at the start and in the middle but near the end it started to be a slog. You can't really rebuild your towers on every map, so you have to take them with you. Which means dragging each individual tower onto your platform and off it after you arrive. This takes longer than it should. Add to it clearing the map from enemies at the start of each map and it becomes very tedious to change maps in later game, especially with the enemies seeming to scale faster than your weapons (I guess you could do better than me, but it was my experience. And if you wanted to just quickly jump between maps to get one specific resource - it feels even worse. Overall an interesting concept and good enough time. But I would like to see some improvements. Like an ability to move towers in bulk at least. I guess changing how upgrades work is not really something that can be done when the game was already released.

Dream Engines: Nomad Cities is a city-building survival strategy game developed by Suncrash and published by Suncrash alongside Gamera Games, blending automation management, exploration, combat, and resource logistics into a distinctive experience centered around mobility. While many city builders focus on constructing massive settlements designed to stand permanently against hardship, this game approaches survival from an entirely different angle. Your city is not meant to remain in one place forever. Instead, it exists as a massive flying fortress capable of lifting off and traveling to safer territory when danger becomes too great. Set within a ruined world consumed by strange corruption and nightmarish threats, the game places players in control of one of humanity’s last hopes for survival. Civilization no longer thrives through expansion alone. Adaptation becomes the most important skill. The hostile landscape constantly pressures players to gather resources, establish production systems, defend citizens, and eventually relocate before overwhelming dangers arrive. That simple idea changes the entire rhythm of city building and creates a strategic identity that feels remarkably different from many competitors in the genre. The city management systems offer familiar foundations while introducing fresh complications. Food production, housing, workforce allocation, and industrial development all require careful attention. Building an efficient settlement involves creating resource chains that support long-term sustainability while maintaining enough flexibility to respond to emergencies. Factories convert raw materials into advanced products, infrastructure expands production capabilities, and workers must remain supplied if growth is going to continue. Automation becomes increasingly important as settlements expand. Early progression focuses heavily on survival and stability, but later stages demand efficient production networks capable of supporting larger populations and more demanding industries. Watching previously chaotic systems evolve into streamlined production lines creates the kind of satisfaction that management game enthusiasts often seek. Optimizing transportation routes, balancing supply demands, and refining industrial layouts become rewarding challenges that continually encourage improvement. The flying city mechanic elevates everything. Traditional city builders often revolve around maximizing a single location, but Dream Engines constantly asks players to think about movement and adaptation. Remaining too long in one region invites escalating danger. Resources eventually become limited. Hostile creatures grow more aggressive. Players must decide when to stay and strengthen defenses or when to abandon established territory entirely in pursuit of survival elsewhere. That constant pressure creates meaningful decisions throughout the entire experience. Expanding rapidly can accelerate progress but increase vulnerability. Overcommitting to one region may leave infrastructure exposed to threats that eventually become impossible to manage. The need to relocate turns city planning into a balancing act between efficiency and mobility, forcing players to think beyond immediate goals. Exploration introduces another valuable layer to progression. Outside the city itself, players can venture into dangerous environments to gather materials and uncover opportunities hidden throughout the world. A customizable Steam-Bot acts as an exploration tool and combat unit, allowing players to engage directly with hostile environments instead of managing everything entirely from a strategic overhead perspective. Combat systems create additional tension by ensuring survival never feels guaranteed. Nightmarish enemies regularly threaten settlements, forcing players to establish defenses and prepare for escalating attacks. Defensive planning becomes a necessity rather than an optional feature. Walls, fortifications, and intelligent layouts contribute heavily to long-term success. Even strong defenses eventually face limits, reinforcing the core philosophy that survival often depends on knowing when to escape rather than simply standing your ground. Progression systems continuously reward experimentation and specialization. New technologies improve infrastructure, strengthen defenses, and unlock increasingly advanced capabilities. Steam-Bot upgrades further expand player options by supporting different combat and exploration styles. These systems create satisfying long-term goals while allowing players to gradually shape strategies around personal preferences. Visually, Dream Engines succeeds in creating a memorable atmosphere. The combination of industrial machinery, floating settlements, ruined landscapes, and supernatural corruption gives the world a distinctive identity. The visual design supports the gameplay effectively by reinforcing the feeling of surviving within an unstable world where danger constantly exists beyond city walls. The game does ask players to invest time into understanding its systems. Newcomers to automation-heavy management titles may initially feel overwhelmed by balancing resource production, infrastructure planning, defense preparation, and exploration simultaneously. The number of moving parts increases substantially during later stages, creating complexity that rewards patience but may intimidate less experienced players. Despite those challenges, Dream Engines: Nomad Cities stands out because it fully embraces its central concept and builds meaningful mechanics around it. The flying city idea could have easily become a simple gimmick, but instead it influences nearly every aspect of gameplay. Resource planning, expansion decisions, defense strategies, and exploration priorities all revolve around mobility and survival. The result is a city-building experience that feels ambitious, creative, and consistently engaging. By combining automation systems with survival pressure and mobile settlement management, Dream Engines offers something refreshingly different within a crowded strategy genre. Players who enjoy logistics management, survival mechanics, and city builders that encourage adaptability will likely find considerable value in its unique design philosophy. Rating: 7/10

While I would love to give this game glowing praise Since I do like it I would give it a 75/100 I can only highlight the positives and negatives and the issues with some of the reviews I read. The positive: -Unique, the concept of moving the base constantly to escape the increasing difficulty is a nice one that forces the player to adapt to new resources and redesign their micro factory to build the things that map can make. -Difficulty, is entirely player dictated with options for most features, you can set the classics like permadeath but also things like base map difficulty rising over time, production speed and much more. The difficulty also only really affects the score you get at the end of a successful or failed run. -The art style is nice, the 3D models look just like the splash art with a touch of Texturing that makes them look weathered or badly painted that reminds me of water colors. The buildings are animated like Factorio if slightly more cartoonishly and with a reliance on smoke for some. The Avatar "Tiny" fits the style of the buildings and enemies, the world looks like it fits to itself. -Tutorial explains what you need to know for basic play. -Story, the setting is interesting and the story follows the discovery of the city itself and research into why it was abandoned. It is interesting and fleshes out the world fairly well. -Factory building, this is genre specific, not everyone's cup of tea but because you have to engage with constant redesigns of your mobile base instead of being able to keep everything and expand endlessly I find it defeats issues games like Factorio and Satisfactory run into. They have to make the amount of resources you need grow endlessly because otherwise I could just build one factory producing each resource and be done with it. Dream Engines takes the approach of small amounts but you have limited time to produce them and which you can produce is location and chosen tribe/upgrades dependant. -The Tribes: lots of large changes created by which you pick, some will see you staying on a map for long periods but movement costs a lot while others will see you constantly map hopping to hover up bonuses from ruins. The Bad: -Combat is a little dry, enemies have a single pattern, close the distance and attack, ranged from further but otherwise no difference. I have read a review comparing it to RiftBreaker but I disagree with the review which said Riftbreaker is way better. I found Riftbreaker to equally fall into mostly endless kiting regardless of loadout choice since the more interesting weapons don't have enough variation to make them viable, damage types are more varied in it forcing you to switch between two types with small usage of elements but ultimately you can beat all of Rift breaker with Chainguns and missle launchers on hardest. Ammo limits and production was a good idea for that one to force melee fighting. Neither is your vampire survivors of infinite attack patterns and choice paralysis. Intelligent enemies forming battle lines instead of just endlessly increasing enemy strength would fix it. more variation of movement styles for non-intelligent and an overhaul of the turrets since I find myself just maxing preparing a big block of the cheapest turrets with a single wall piece around it while I dance Tiny in front as bait the enemies preferentially attack during raids. That said in Rift breaker I just cheesed each map by constructing a defense line around the entire perimeter. once I figured this out the game became such a slog, most of my "gameplay" was waiting around for things to produce. Because of the nomadic nature no such one and done tactic exists for Dream Engines. Sometimes I have to create multiple defense lines because there isn't enough space in one direction to build my death disco so enemies overwhelm me forcing a retreat and then they start breaking my walls. -Difficulty, yup the duality, the biggest issue with the difficult is also its greatest strength: open difficult. Since you can set any difficulty you want and the game defaults pretty high, you get people complaining about the difficulty even while accidentally selecting Normal which has growing difficulty set to on. This setting isn't really a beginner setting. If forces the player to be much more efficient then any other single option does. Since if I am not ready for the next base map difficulty, without it, I can just endlessly harvest resources and upgrades. With it I need a rare consumable that lowers 1 level every 200 cycles. With even short stays on a map being around 30 cycles. Otherwise I will be pushed into a difficulty I can't yet survive. -The lack of modularity while appearing to have modularity. While the tribes do a good job changing gameplay... there is no reason to, just find your preferred one and stick to it... if there was say a home base to return to and you made upgrades to improve your future runs with a wide variety of environments each tribe accelled with or were exclusive to and so exclusive resources. Then you would have reason to change but there isn't. While mods exist for buildings and Tiny, Tiny has a single port for mods and the selection basically limits you to speed, auto repair or a tiny area of splash damage. The defense and offense improving ones counter act each other making them basically non-choices since dodging is better then defense and Tiny is too squishy for melee. The city has very few mod slots and instead every single building gets at least one... in which to put your 1 or 2 mods per building type in dozens of turrets that could be destroyed or around 2-4 of each production building... That don't fundamentally change how well they perform. There is a general upkeep mod but the amount it reduces is so minimal of things you can easily get that it should have just been a crafting recipe of high expense item that would feel inferior to material need or personel reduction mods but ocassionally useful. There are a few that speed up production at material expense or lower material usage at production speed expense... none for more people but better production or material use or any mixture like that or specific material use... Giving you batches of 5 of those would make them much more worthwhile as would more affected stats at once and variety. The city mods are extremely useful but the mod slots are not particularly numerous, limit you to 1 per type and most of them have no drawbacks or secondary effects you could juggle and match together for slight improvements with no downsides. Instead you are most likely to use cart speed 1 and 2 or cart speed 2 and attention reduction. The weapons don't have modularity, most are rare finds from ruins and aren't seperated into tiers other then in material needs to produce them. The ones you can research and then produce are limited to certain effects while things like piercing are locked behind the lucky pulls. There are no enemy damage types so no armor types either, just how much health they give versus regen and speed. No attack or fire rate bonuses either. Tooltips of items and buildings don't say enough, in part this is because buildings have levels and mods can change them and multiple recipes but a quality of life that would also let you show some information would be to immediately build them at a specific level and mods and show selectable recipe production rate. While the negative reviews do the game a disservice from the ones I read they aren't wrong about issues that could be fixed with some work. The game is otherwise very solid for an indie studio with 3 people, I hope they are doing well! while both their games lack polish they are interesting and could be incredibly deep if given that polish.
